title: The developer's job: what you are actually paid to do
summary: A developer is paid last: profit is the residual left after every other party is paid. That residual moves on four levers — income, cost, time and the market's multiple — and it is protected by go/no-go gates whose criteria are written before the money is spent.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the developer is the person paid last. Profit is whatever is left after everyone else has been paid, so your job is to control the few things that decide that residual, and to decide early, against criteria you wrote down before you spent the money, whether to keep going.

Why this matters

Every other seat at a development table has a contract that pays it first. The lender is paid interest every month. The contractor is paid against monthly progress. The architect and engineers are paid fees by stage. The broker is paid a commission at closing. The municipality collects its permit fees before it issues a permit. You, the developer, are paid only if the finished building is worth more than everything it cost, and only after all of them. That makes you the one person whose income is a difference rather than a fee. A person paid by a difference has to think differently from everyone around them, because they are the only one exposed to how small that difference really is.

Paid last: profit is the residual

In plain English: you take everything the finished project is worth, subtract everything it cost, and what remains is yours. Nobody guarantees that remainder. It can be large, it can be zero, and it can be negative.

The professional framing is that development profit is the completed value minus the total development cost, where total cost includes land, construction, professional fees, permits, financing costs and contingency. A residual is simply what is left over after fixed claims are paid. The important property of a residual is leverage: because it is a small difference between two large numbers, a small percentage change in either large number becomes a large percentage change in the remainder.

Here is the worked example. This is hypothetical. A 60-unit apartment building costs $14 million to deliver, all in. Once leased, it is worth $16 million. Profit is $2 million.

  • Suppose rents come in 5 percent below plan, so the building is worth 5 percent less: $15.2 million. Profit falls from $2 million to $1.2 million. A 5 percent miss on income has cut your profit by 40 percent.
  • Suppose instead construction overruns by 10 percent. Cost rises from $14 million to $15.4 million. Profit falls to $0.6 million. A 10 percent overrun has cut your profit by 70 percent.

Nobody on the contractor's side of the table lost 70 percent of anything. Only you did. That is what being paid last means.

The four levers

Four things move the residual, and you should be able to name them in your sleep: income, cost, time and the market's multiple.

Income is what the building earns: rent, or sale prices, less vacancy. Cost is everything you spend to deliver it. Time is how long all of it takes; every extra month costs interest, insurance, site overhead and your own attention, and it pushes your sale into a market you cannot yet see. The multiple is what buyers will pay for each dollar of a building's yearly net operating income (NOI), which is rent collected minus the costs of operating the building, before debt payments.

In the example, the building earns NOI of $1 million a year and the market pays 16 times that, so it is worth $16 million. Investors usually quote the inverse of the multiple, called the capitalisation rate; you will meet it properly in week 10. For now, think of the multiple as the market's mood about your kind of building.

Second worked example, same hypothetical building. Nothing changes in your rents or your costs. But interest rates rise, buyers become cautious, and the multiple falls from 16 to 14. Your $1 million of NOI is now worth $14 million. That is exactly what the building cost. Your $2 million profit is gone, and you did nothing wrong on site.

Notice the difference in control. You influence income through design, product and leasing. You influence cost through scope, procurement and discipline. You control time more than any other lever, because most delay begins with a decision that was not made. The multiple you do not control at all; you only control how exposed you are to it, through timing, through how much you borrow, and through whether you can afford to wait.

The lifecycle: risk is highest when money is lowest

A project moves through stages: finding the idea and the site, testing feasibility, securing approvals, designing, financing, building, leasing or selling, and finally holding or exiting. The cruel fact of the lifecycle is that the uncertainty is greatest at the start, when you have spent almost nothing, and the spending is greatest at the end, when most of the uncertainty has already resolved.

StageUncertaintyMoney committed
Idea and site searchVery highVery low
Feasibility and due diligenceHighLow
Land purchase and approvalsFallingRising sharply
ConstructionLower, but now expensiveMost of the budget

The practical consequence is that early dollars buy the most information. A few thousand dollars spent on a zoning check, a soil report or a frank conversation with a lender can tell you whether a $14 million project should exist. The same dollars spent in month eighteen buy almost nothing, because by then you are committed.

Say that out loud now.

Go/no-go gates, written before the spend

A gate is a fixed point where you stop and decide, deliberately, whether to commit the next tranche of money. A go/no-go gate has written criteria, decided before the spending, that tell you what you must see to proceed. If the criteria are met, you go. If they are not, you stop, or you redesign and come back to the gate.

The criteria must be written before the spend because afterwards your judgment is contaminated. Once you have paid for drawings, you want the drawings to be worth something. Once you have told people about the project, you want it to happen. Writing the bar first is how you protect a future decision from your future self.

An applied example. Before you sign a binding land purchase, a sensible first gate might require: zoning confirmed in writing to permit the intended use and density; a cost estimate from a qualified cost consultant; a projected profit at or above a minimum you set in advance; a realistic schedule; and at least one lender willing to discuss terms in writing. Those thresholds are your commercial choices, not standards. If any criterion fails, the land deal waits or dies.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is momentum. Every week of work creates people who want the project to proceed: consultants with more fees ahead, a broker waiting on a commission, and you, with your name attached. The control is to write the gate criteria before the spending, sign them, and give someone the explicit duty to say no if the criteria are not met. On a small team, that someone may be an outside adviser whose fee does not depend on the answer.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner falls in love with the building and treats the financial model as a sales document. He looks at profit in dollars, never in percentages, and never asks what a 5 percent miss does to it. The professional looks at the same model as a list of things that can go wrong, and asks of each number: who controls this, and how wrong could it be?

Callback

This is the first lesson, so the callback is to your own work. In grid operations, the limits are set before the event. A reliability coordinator does not renegotiate a thermal limit while the line is sagging; the limit was studied in advance, written down and agreed, precisely so that nobody has to invent it under pressure. Go/no-go gates are the development version of operating limits.

Recap

The developer is paid last, so profit is a residual, and a residual swings hard. Four levers move it: income, cost, time and the market's multiple, and only the first three are yours to steer. Risk is highest when spending is lowest, so early money buys the most information. Gates with written criteria, decided before the spend, are how you keep momentum from making your decisions for you.

Next: Ford, Failure Forensics — Berlin Brandenburg Airport, the building that skipped its gates.
checklist: Write the four levers on the first page of every project file: income, cost, time and the market's multiple.
Run three sensitivities on every pro forma: income down 5 percent, cost up 10 percent, multiple down two turns.
Express profit as a percentage of cost as well as in dollars.
Name the gates for the project and write each gate's criteria before the spend it controls.
Spend early money on information: zoning, soils, cost and a lender's view.
Give someone whose fee does not depend on the answer the explicit duty to say no.
Record which levers you control, which you influence, and which you only manage exposure to.
head: Field checklist
speak: The developer is paid last. The lender, the contractor, the consultants and the city are all paid first, and what is left is mine. That residual swings hard, because it is a small difference between two big numbers. On a hypothetical building costing fourteen million and worth sixteen, a five percent miss on income cuts profit by forty percent, a ten percent cost overrun cuts it by seventy percent, and a fall in the market's multiple from sixteen to fourteen wipes it out. So I watch four levers: income, cost, time and the multiple. I steer the first three; I can only manage my exposure to the fourth. Because risk is highest when I have spent least, early money buys the most information. And at each stage I stop at a go/no-go gate whose criteria I wrote before spending a dollar, so momentum never decides for me.
terms: Residual — what is left after every fixed claim has been paid; a developer's profit is a residual.
Net operating income (NOI) — a building's rent collected minus its operating costs, before any debt payments.
Go/no-go gate — a fixed decision point where written criteria, set before the spending, decide whether the next tranche of money is committed.

hostile.q: Your profit is two million on fourteen million of cost. What happens to my loan if you are ten percent over budget?
hostile.a: A ten percent overrun is $1.4 million, which cuts my profit to $0.6 million, so I do not rely on profit to absorb it. The budget carries a contingency sized at the gate, the overrun is funded by equity ahead of your loan, and I will show you the sensitivity table so you can see the cushion at each step.

title: Berlin Brandenburg Airport: the building that skipped its gates
summary: Berlin Brandenburg Airport began construction in 2006, cancelled a June 2012 opening weeks beforehand because its fire and smoke system could not be approved, and opened on 31 October 2020. The root cause was an owner acting as integrator without the capability to do it, approving changes with no gate on them, and holding a public date it had not earned.
body:
Berlin Brandenburg Airport opened eight years after the date it had announced. The building was not the root problem. The owner chose to coordinate the job itself without the capability, kept approving changes with no gate on them, and held a public opening date it had not earned. One rule comes out of it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will be the owner on your own projects. This case is about what owners do, not what contractors do. Every decision that broke this airport was an owner's decision, and every one of them has a small-project version that you could make next year on a 20-unit building. The scale is different. The pattern is identical.

Failure forensics is the discipline of taking a real failure apart in a fixed order, so that you learn the mechanism instead of the headline. We use seven steps every time: timeline, key decisions, assumptions, incentives, warning signs ignored, point of no return, and root cause. Then we write one prevention rule. The order matters: we refuse to name a root cause until we have looked at decisions, assumptions and incentives, because the first explanation people reach for is usually the most visible one, not the deepest.

Step 1: Timeline

Construction of the new airport for Berlin began in 2006. The owner was a company held by public shareholders, the states of Berlin and Brandenburg and the federal government. An opening was set for June 2012, publicly announced, with the move of airlines and staff planned around it. Weeks before that date, in May 2012, the opening was cancelled, because the building's fire and smoke-control system could not be approved by the authorities for use. The airport finally opened on 31 October 2020. Costs grew to several times the original budget along the way; this lesson does not quote a figure, because the published numbers depend on what is counted.

Step 2: Key decisions

  • The owner chose to coordinate many separate construction packages itself, rather than hand the integration of the whole building to one party with the experience to do it.
  • The owner kept approving design and scope changes while construction was underway, so the building being built kept changing.
  • The owner announced, and then defended, a public opening date.

Step 3: Assumptions

Three assumptions sit under those decisions. First, that coordinating packages yourself saves money, because you avoid paying a single contractor's margin for integration. Second, that changes can be absorbed as they arrive. Third, that a date, once announced, can be met by pressure. All three are common, and all three are wrong in the same way: each treats integration as free. On a complex building, integration is the hardest and most expensive work there is. The fire and smoke system is the clearest example. It touches architecture, structure, mechanical systems, electrical systems and controls, and it must work as one system to be approved.

Step 4: Incentives

Look at who was paid for what. Each package contractor was responsible for its own package, and paid for its own scope. Changes typically bring additional payment, so a change is rarely bad news for the party carrying it out. Public owners face pressure to show progress, and an announced date is a political commitment as much as a technical one. No party at the table was paid to make the whole thing work together except the owner, and the owner did not have the team to do it. When nobody is paid for the whole, the whole is nobody's job.

Say that out loud now.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

Changes keep arriving during construction. Interfaces between packages generate disputes over who is responsible for what. Testing and commissioning, the work of proving that systems actually perform, is squeezed toward the end because everything before it ran late. Any one of those, on its own, is a signal that the date is not earned. Together they are a forecast. The lesson here is not that someone missed one subtle clue; it is that the clues were the ordinary signs of a project losing control, and the date held anyway.

Step 6: Point of no return

The point of no return was not May 2012. By then the outcome was already decided. It came earlier, when the owner committed to coordinating the work itself and kept accepting changes without a gate to stop them. After that, every month added complexity to a building whose integration nobody fully controlled. Cancelling the opening weeks before the date was not the failure; it was the moment the failure became visible.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause was an owner acting as the integrator of a complex building without the capability to do it, with no gate on changes. The cancelled date was a symptom. A public date that had not been earned, defended for too long, made the symptom expensive and humiliating.

Be precise about what the root cause is not. It is not that one engineer designed one system badly, and it is not bad luck. A different fire system design, delivered into the same structure of ownership and change, would have met a different version of the same fate. Root cause means the condition which, if removed, would have prevented the whole family of failures, not just the one that happened to surface first. That is why the prevention rule below is about gates, not about smoke extraction.

Two applied examples at your scale

This is a composite example. A developer building a 30-unit apartment building hires the excavator, the concrete trade, the framer and the mechanical trade directly, to save a general contractor's fee. Each trade finishes its own work. Nobody owns the sequence between them. The mechanical trade finds its ducts clash with beams the framer has already installed, and each blames the other. The developer, who has a full-time job elsewhere, is now the integrator by default. The fee he saved is spent many times over in rework and delay.

A second composite. A developer tells a lender and fifty pre-sale buyers that the building will be ready in September. In June the fire alarm and sprinkler contractors are behind, and the building inspector has not yet seen the system tested. The developer pushes everyone to hit September because he said September. The right move was to say, in June, that the date depends on passing final inspections, and to give a date that was conditional on those results.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is letting an outside commitment move you past a gate. A date you announced, a story you told a lender, money already spent: none of them change whether the building is ready. The control is that each gate, including the one before you announce a date, has written criteria, and only those criteria open it. On a building, the final gate before occupancy should require that life-safety systems have passed testing and been accepted by the authority.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks being the integrator is free because it does not appear as a line in the budget. It does appear, later, as delay, rework and claims. If you will coordinate the work yourself, decide that deliberately, and staff it with people who have done it before. If you cannot, pay someone whose job is the whole building.

Callback

In lesson 1, Remi said the developer is paid last and that gates with written criteria protect a decision from momentum. Berlin is what momentum looks like at full scale. A date was announced, changes kept coming, and the gate that should have asked whether the building was ready to be tested was never treated as a gate at all.

Recap

The airport opened eight years late because the owner coordinated packages without the capability, approved changes with no gate, and defended a public date it had not earned. The fire and smoke system failing approval was the symptom. The rule: no date, announcement or sunk cost moves me past a gate; only the gate's written criteria do.

Next: Sage, The Money — where the money sits: profit on cost, the equity cheque and money committed by stage.
checklist: Decide in writing who integrates the whole building, and confirm they have done it before.
Put a gate on every design or scope change after construction starts: who approved it, what it costs in money and time.
Never announce a date that has not passed its gate; give conditional dates instead.
Make life-safety testing and acceptance a written criterion of the final gate before occupancy.
Track interface disputes between trades as a warning sign, not an annoyance.
Protect time for testing and commissioning at the end of the schedule.
Run the seven forensic steps on any failure you study: timeline, decisions, assumptions, incentives, warning signs, point of no return, root cause.
head: Field checklist
speak: Berlin Brandenburg Airport began construction in 2006 and was due to open in June 2012. Weeks before, the opening was cancelled because the fire and smoke-control system could not be approved. It finally opened on 31 October 2020. The fire system was the symptom, not the cause. The owner chose to coordinate many construction packages itself without the capability to integrate them, kept approving changes with no gate to stop them, and held a public date it had not earned. Nobody at the table was paid to make the whole building work except the owner, and the owner did not have the team. The point of no return was not the cancellation; it was the earlier decision to be the integrator with no control on change. My rule from this case: no date, announcement or sunk cost moves me past a gate. Only the gate's written criteria do.
terms: Integrator — the party responsible for making all the separately built parts of a project work together as one building.
Commissioning — the process of testing building systems to prove they perform as designed, before handover.
Point of no return — the decision after which the eventual outcome was effectively fixed, often well before the failure becomes visible.

hostile.q: You plan to hire the trades directly and save the general contractor's fee. Who carries the risk of everything falling between the packages?
hostile.a: I do, which is why I have not decided it yet. Either I put an experienced construction manager on the job whose scope is the whole building, with interfaces assigned in writing, or I pay a general contractor to carry them. I will not be the integrator by default.

rule: Rule 1: No date, announcement or sunk cost moves me past a gate. Only the gate's written criteria do.

title: Where the money sits: profit on cost, the equity cheque and money committed by stage
summary: Profit only means something as a percentage of what is at risk. Profit on cost measures the project; return on equity measures what the residual does to your own cheque, and debt makes that swing harder. Money committed rises sharply after the land closes, so the cheapest spending is the information you buy before it.
body:
A profit figure in dollars tells you almost nothing. Express it against the cost at risk, then against your own equity, and you see what the four levers really do to you. And because your money goes in fastest once the land closes, the best dollars you will ever spend are the ones before it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, lenders and investors will not ask you how much you expect to make. They will ask what your profit is as a share of cost, how much of your own money is in, and when it goes in. Those three questions decide whether they fund you, and they are the same three questions that decide whether you should fund yourself. This lesson gives you the three views in order: the project, your cheque, and the calendar.

Profit on cost and margin on value

In plain English: two million dollars of profit is excellent on a five million dollar project and thin on a fifty million dollar one. So we divide.

The professional framing uses two ratios. Profit on cost is profit divided by total development cost. Margin on value is profit divided by completed value. They describe the same project from opposite ends.

Worked example one, using the hypothetical building from lesson 1: cost $14 million, value $16 million, profit $2 million.

  • Profit on cost: $2 million divided by $14 million equals 0.143, or 14.3 percent.
  • Margin on value: $2 million divided by $16 million equals 0.125, or 12.5 percent.

Profit on cost is the number a developer and a lender usually watch, because it tells you how much the cost can rise before the profit is gone. At 14.3 percent, a cost overrun of about 14.3 percent eats the whole profit. Any minimum you set for this ratio is a commercial choice, not a standard; markets and lenders set their own expectations, and they move.

Now read the cushion against the quality of the estimate. A cost estimate prepared from a sketch is far less certain than one prepared from finished drawings and contractor prices. Early in a project, a 14 percent cushion can be smaller than the honest uncertainty in the estimate itself. So the same profit on cost is comfortable at one stage and alarming at another. A professional always asks two questions together: how big is the cushion, and how good is the number it is measured against? Sage will return to estimate quality in week 13; for now, simply never quote a profit on cost without saying what stage of estimate it rests on.

The equity cheque: why your money feels every percent twice

Most development is funded partly by borrowed money and partly by equity, which is the owner's own money that sits behind the debt and absorbs losses first. Because the lender is paid before you, every dollar of loss lands on the equity first.

Worked example two, still hypothetical. The $14 million cost is funded 65 percent by a construction loan and 35 percent by equity. The loan is $9.1 million; the equity is $4.9 million. To keep this simple, ignore the time value of money for now; Priya and Nadia will add it in later weeks.

  • Base case: profit of $2 million on equity of $4.9 million is a 40.8 percent return over the life of the project.
  • Now the 10 percent overrun from lesson 1. Construction lenders commonly require cost increases to be funded by the owner rather than by more loan, which is a commercial practice, not a rule. So equity rises by $1.4 million to $6.3 million, and profit falls to $0.6 million. Return on equity falls to 0.6 divided by 6.3, which is 9.5 percent.

The same overrun that cut project profit by 70 percent cut your return on your own money from about 41 percent to about 10 percent, and it also asked you for $1.4 million more cash at the worst possible moment. That second effect is the one that sinks small developers. They do not run out of profit; they run out of cash.

Say that out loud now.

Money committed by stage

The third view is time. Write down, for each stage, how much money you have spent and how much you are legally committed to spend. A hypothetical spending profile for the same building:

StageSpent at end of stageShare of total cost
Feasibility and due diligence$150,000About 1 percent
Land purchase closed$2,650,000About 19 percent
Design and approvals complete$3,350,000About 24 percent
Construction contract signed$3,350,000 spent, plus the full contract committedMost of the cost is now committed

Two things leap out. First, spent and committed are different. The day you sign a construction contract, you may have spent a quarter of the budget but you have committed nearly all of it. Second, the jump at land closing is enormous. Before closing, your exposure was $150,000 of studies. After it, your exposure is the land, and land is hard to sell quickly at full price.

Committed also includes deposits you could forfeit and contracts you cannot cancel without paying. Some consultants' agreements, for example, allow termination only on notice with payment for work to date, while a land deposit may be lost entirely if you walk away. When you build your spending table, add a column for what it would cost to stop at each point. That column, not the spent column, is your real exposure.

That is why the cheapest money you will ever spend is the money before the land closes. A zoning letter, a soil investigation, a frank cost estimate and a lender's first reaction together cost a small fraction of the land, and they are the information that decides whether the land should be bought at all.

How the best do it

Large institutional developers commonly fund the pursuit of a new project from a small, separate budget that is released in tranches. Each tranche is approved by an investment committee only after the previous tranche has produced the evidence it was meant to buy. The pursuit budget is expected to lose money on most sites, because most sites should be abandoned. What a small developer can copy is the structure, not the size: a fixed pursuit budget per site, released in steps, with a written list of what each step must prove, and the acceptance that walking away after spending it is a success, not a failure.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is equity exhaustion: an overrun or delay that demands more cash than you have, mid-construction, when the lender will not advance more and the half-built building cannot be sold for what it cost. The control is a written liquidity plan at the financing gate: how much additional equity you can produce, from where, how quickly, and what you will do if the contingency is used up.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner looks at the return on equity in the base case, 40 percent in our example, and stops reading. The professional reads the base case last. He looks first at the overrun case and the delay case, then at the cash call each one triggers, and only then at the headline.

Callback

The callback is to your grid work. A system operator does not ask only how much load the network carries today; he asks how much reserve remains if the largest single unit trips. Your equity is that reserve. Profit on cost tells you the margin; your liquidity plan tells you whether you survive the trip.

Recap

Express profit against cost, and against your equity. Profit on cost tells you how much cost can rise before profit is gone; return on equity shows that debt makes every miss land twice on your cheque, and that overruns usually arrive as cash calls. Money committed jumps at land closing and again at the construction contract, so buy your information before those two moments.

Next: REGA, The Rules — the gates the government holds: permits, inspections and the certificate of occupancy.
checklist: State profit three ways on every pro forma: dollars, profit on cost, and return on equity.
Compute how large an overrun eats the whole profit.
Write a liquidity plan before the financing gate: how much extra equity, from where, how fast.
Track spent and committed separately for every stage.
Fix a pursuit budget per site and release it in tranches tied to evidence.
Buy zoning, soils, cost and lender information before the land closes.
Read the downside cases before the base case.
head: Field checklist
speak: A profit in dollars means little until I divide it. Profit on cost tells me how far cost can rise before profit is gone; on a hypothetical fourteen million dollar building with two million of profit, that cushion is about fourteen percent. Then I look at my own cheque. If the project is sixty-five percent debt and thirty-five percent equity, the lender is paid first, so every loss lands on my equity first. A ten percent overrun cuts my return on equity from about forty-one percent to under ten, and it arrives as a cash call of 1.4 million dollars in the middle of construction. Developers rarely run out of profit first; they run out of cash. Finally I watch time: money committed jumps when the land closes and again when the construction contract is signed. So the cheapest money I will ever spend is the information I buy before the land closes.
terms: Profit on cost — development profit divided by total development cost; it shows how much cost can rise before profit disappears.
Equity — the owner's own money in a project, which sits behind the debt and absorbs losses first.
Committed cost — money you are legally obliged to spend, whether or not it has been paid yet.

hostile.q: Your base case shows a forty percent return on equity. If you are ten percent over, where does the extra cash come from, and how fast?
hostile.a: The overrun on this hypothetical budget is $1.4 million. The contingency covers the first part; the remainder comes from committed equity identified in my liquidity plan, which I can show you, and which is available within the draw cycle. If that fails, the plan sets out what scope I cut first.

title: The gates the government holds: permits, inspections and the certificate of occupancy
summary: The law puts its own gates into every project: land-use approval, the building permit, inspections during construction and permission to occupy. You do not control their criteria or their timing, so your own gates must sit in front of them, and your schedule must treat them as risks rather than dates.
body:
Some gates in your project are not yours. The government holds them: permission to use the land, permission to build, inspection while you build, and permission to occupy. You cannot set their criteria or their timing, so your own gates must sit in front of theirs, and your schedule must treat each one as a risk, not as a date.

Recall

Q. Why is a developer's profit described as a residual?

A. Because it is what is left after every other party, from the lender to the contractor to the city, has been paid; it is a small difference between two large numbers, so it swings hard.

Q. What was Rule 1?

A. No date, announcement or sunk cost moves me past a gate. Only the gate's written criteria do.

Q. Why is the cheapest money the money before land closes?

A. Because exposure jumps at closing, and studies before it cost a small fraction of the land while deciding whether the land should be bought.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, at Berlin the fire and smoke system could not be approved, and a whole airport stood empty. The government's gate did exactly what it exists to do: it refused to let people occupy a building whose life-safety systems had not been shown to work. Your projects will pass through the same kinds of gates. Knowing what they are, who holds them and what they need is basic owner competence. This lesson teaches the general pattern. The specific approvals, fees, timelines and criteria depend on the jurisdiction, so verify each against the primary source before you rely on it.

The four public gates

In plain English, a typical project needs permission four times.

  1. Land use. Is this use, at this size, allowed on this land? This is zoning or planning, and sometimes a separate site plan or development approval.
  2. Building permit. Do the drawings show a building that meets the adopted building code? The building department reviews the plans before work starts.
  3. Inspections. Was it actually built the way the approved drawings show? Inspectors visit at defined stages, and some work cannot be covered up until it is inspected.
  4. Occupancy. Is the finished building safe to use? The building official issues a certificate of occupancy, a document permitting people to use the building for its approved purpose.

The professional framing uses one more term: the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ), meaning the official or office with legal power to approve, inspect or enforce a particular requirement. A single project often has several: a planning department, a building department, a fire marshal, a utility, sometimes an environmental agency. Part of early due diligence is simply drawing the map of which authority holds which gate. A short meeting with the planning and building departments before you buy, where that is offered, is often the cheapest information on the whole project.

The code is adopted, not just written

In American practice, model codes such as the International Building Code (IBC), published by the International Code Council, become law only when a state or local government adopts them, usually a specific edition, often with local amendments. So the question is never just "what does the IBC say?" It is "which edition has this jurisdiction adopted, and what did it change?" A design that meets one edition may not meet the adopted one.

The model codes also place duties on the owner, not only on the designer and builder. For example, the IBC's special inspection provisions generally require the owner, or an agent acting for the owner, to engage special inspectors for certain critical work such as structural concrete and steel, rather than leaving it to the contractor. Verify that against the current adopted edition before you rely on it. The point is that you are not a bystander in the code; you have obligations of your own.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example one: placing your gates in front of theirs

This is hypothetical. You find a site and want to build 40 apartments. The current zoning appears to allow 30. You can buy the land three ways: unconditionally, with a condition that you obtain the approval for 40 units before you must close, or with an option to buy later.

  • Unconditional purchase puts the government's gate after your money. If the approval is refused, you own land for 30 units at a price you set for 40.
  • A conditional purchase or option puts the government's gate in front of your money. You may pay more, or pay a deposit you could lose, but your largest commitment waits until the public gate has opened.

Your gate criterion becomes: "We do not close on the land until the land-use approval for 40 units is granted and any appeal period has passed." Whether a seller will accept that, and what appeal periods apply, are commercial and legal questions for your lawyer. Professional sign-off required: real estate lawyer.

Worked example two: inspections as hold points

A hypothetical concrete floor. The rebar is placed; the inspector must see it before the concrete is poured, because afterwards nobody can. If the pour is scheduled for Tuesday and the inspection is not booked, the crew either waits, which costs money, or pours without inspection, which can mean breaking out concrete later or failing the occupancy gate. The owner's control is simple: every inspection required by the permit is a line in the schedule with a named person responsible for booking it, and no covering work proceeds until it is signed off. Professional sign-off required: engineer of record for the structural work.

What the occupancy gate actually asks

The final public gate is the one most beginners underestimate, because it comes last and feels like paperwork. It is not. Before a certificate of occupancy is issued, the building official typically needs final inspections passed across disciplines, and the fire authority typically needs life-safety systems such as fire alarms, sprinklers and smoke control tested and accepted. Those tests depend on systems being complete, powered and working together, which is precisely the stage at which late projects cut corners. The details vary by jurisdiction; verify them against the primary source before you rely on them. The owner's lesson is to plan backwards from occupancy: list what the authorities will need to see, and protect the time to show it to them. Professional sign-off required: fire protection engineer.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating a public approval as a date you can schedule rather than an outcome you do not control. Approval timelines vary, conditions can be imposed, and decisions can be appealed. The control is to place your largest commitments after the public gates wherever possible, to carry float in the schedule for approvals, and to keep a register of every permit and inspection with its status.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner assumes the architect or contractor is responsible for approvals and that the owner just signs. Many applications are made in the owner's name, many obligations fall on the owner, and when an approval stalls, it is the owner's money that waits. Know your gates personally.

Callback

In lesson 1, Remi taught that risk is highest when money committed is lowest. The public gates are a large share of that early risk. Land-use approval in particular is one of the biggest uncertainties a project has, and it is resolved before construction money is spent, which is exactly why your own gate criteria should require it to be resolved before you buy.

Recap

The government holds four gates: land use, building permit, inspections and occupancy, each controlled by an authority having jurisdiction. Codes apply only in the edition a jurisdiction has adopted, and they place duties on the owner too. Put your money behind the public gates, schedule them as risks, and track every inspection as a hold point.

Next: Roman, The Numbers — the price of a gate: expected value and what a study is worth.
checklist: Map every authority having jurisdiction for the site and which gate each holds.
Confirm which code edition the jurisdiction has adopted, and its local amendments.
Structure the land deal so the land-use approval comes before your largest commitment, with legal advice.
Keep a permit and inspection register with status and a named owner for each item.
Treat approval durations as risks with float, never as fixed dates.
Confirm in writing who engages special inspectors, and verify the owner's duties against the adopted code.
Allow no covering work until the required inspection is signed off.
head: Field checklist
speak: The government holds four gates in every project. Permission to use the land for what I want. Permission to build, after the plans are reviewed against the adopted code. Inspections while I build, some of which must happen before work is covered. And permission to occupy, the certificate of occupancy. Each is held by an authority having jurisdiction, and a project often has several of them. The building code only applies in the edition my jurisdiction has adopted, with its local changes, and it puts duties on me as owner, not just on my designers. I cannot set the criteria or the timing of these gates, so I put my money behind them. I do not close on land until the approval I need has been granted, I schedule approvals as risks with float, and I track every inspection as a hold point.
terms: Authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) — the official or office with legal power to approve, inspect or enforce a particular requirement.
Certificate of occupancy — the official document permitting a building to be used for its approved purpose.
Adopted code — the specific edition of a model code, with any local amendments, that a jurisdiction has made law.

hostile.q: Your schedule shows the building permit in month four. What happens to my loan if it arrives in month nine?
hostile.a: The permit date in my schedule is a forecast, not a commitment, and it carries float. I do not draw construction funds until the permit is issued, so the delay costs me holding costs on the land, which my budget carries for a defined period. I will show you that period and what I do if the permit runs beyond it.

title: The price of a gate: expected value and what a study is worth
summary: A gate is worth paying for when the information it buys is likely to stop a bad commitment. Expected value lets you put a number on that: compare the project's expected outcome with and without the study, and the difference is the most the study can be worth.
body:
A gate costs money: a study, a delay, a deposit. It is worth paying for when the information it buys is likely to stop you making a bad commitment. Expected value turns that judgment into a number you can write down, defend and check later.

Recall

Q. In lesson 1, what happened to the hypothetical $2 million profit when the multiple fell from 16 to 14?

A. The $1 million of NOI became worth $14 million, equal to the cost, so profit fell to zero.

Q. In lesson 3, what is profit on cost?

A. Development profit divided by total development cost; it shows how far cost can rise before profit is gone.

Q. In lesson 4, why should your land purchase wait for the land-use approval?

A. So the government's gate opens before your largest commitment, rather than after it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, every consultant you meet will tell you their study is essential. Some are. Some are not. You need a way to decide that does not depend on who is most persuasive. Lenders think this way too: they are paying for certainty, and they price it. If you can show the value of the information you bought, you speak their language.

Expected value in plain English

Expected value is the average outcome you would get if you could make the same decision many times. You take each possible outcome, multiply it by its probability, and add the results. It does not predict what will happen this time. It tells you which choice is better on average, so that over a career of decisions you come out ahead.

The probabilities are judgments, not facts. You write them down so they can be challenged before the decision and checked after it. A probability you never wrote down cannot be learned from.

Worked example one: buy now, or study first

This is hypothetical. You are offered a site. Your pro forma shows a profit of $2.0 million if the site is as it appears. Your experienced judgment, written down, is that there is a 25 percent chance of a hidden fatal problem, such as poor soil that needs expensive foundations or a zoning limit tighter than it looks. If you buy and that problem exists, you expect to lose $1.5 million, after selling the site or redesigning a smaller project.

Option A: buy without studying.

  1. Good case: 75 percent probability times $2.0 million profit equals $1.5 million.
  2. Bad case: 25 percent probability times negative $1.5 million equals negative $0.375 million.
  3. Expected value: $1.5 million minus $0.375 million equals $1.125 million.

Option B: spend $120,000 on studies first. Assume, for this example, that the studies reliably reveal the problem if it exists. If they find it, you walk away and lose only the $120,000. If they do not, you proceed, and your profit is reduced by the study cost.

  1. Good case: 75 percent times ($2.0 million minus $0.12 million) equals 0.75 times $1.88 million, which is $1.41 million.
  2. Bad case found in time: 25 percent times negative $0.12 million equals negative $0.03 million.
  3. Expected value: $1.41 million minus $0.03 million equals $1.38 million.

The gate is worth $1.38 million minus $1.125 million, which is $0.255 million, or $255,000 of expected value. You are not spending $120,000; you are buying $375,000 of avoided expected loss for $120,000.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example two: the most a study can be worth

Now ask the reverse question. What is the most you should pay for those studies? Let the cost of the study be c dollars. The expected value with the study is 0.75 times ($2.0 million minus c), plus 0.25 times negative c. That simplifies to $1.5 million minus c. Without the study it was $1.125 million.

The study is worth buying as long as $1.5 million minus c is greater than $1.125 million, which means c must be less than $0.375 million. So in this example, any study costing less than $375,000 that reliably finds the problem is worth paying for. That ceiling is called the expected value of perfect information: the most a decision-maker should pay to remove the uncertainty completely.

Two practical points follow. First, the ceiling grows with the size of the possible loss and the probability of the problem. A cheap study on a risky site is almost always worth it. Second, real studies are not perfect; a soil report can miss a pocket of bad ground. An imperfect study is worth less than the ceiling, so treat the ceiling as an upper bound, not a target.

What the numbers do not do for you

Expected value assumes you can survive the bad case. If losing $1.5 million would end your company, a positive expected value is not enough; you need the bad case to be survivable. This is where risk management differs from arithmetic. A professional checks two things: is the expected value positive, and can I absorb the worst plausible outcome? A decision that fails the second test is declined even when it passes the first.

Think of a coin flip that pays you three times your stake on heads and takes everything you own on tails. The expected value is attractive. Nobody sensible takes the bet, because there is no second flip after tails. Development is full of bets shaped like that, usually disguised as a single large site bought with too much borrowed money.

Also, the probability is the weakest number in the calculation. Ask where it came from. A 25 percent figure based on what happened on similar sites nearby is worth more than one you felt in your stomach. Next week, Kema will teach you how to find that figure properly, using what is called the outside view.

Gates in sequence

A real project has several gates, and the same arithmetic applies at each one. Early gates are cheap and resolve large uncertainties: zoning, soils, market. Later gates are expensive and resolve smaller ones. A useful habit is to order your studies by value per dollar: the cheapest study that could kill the project goes first. If a $5,000 zoning letter could end the deal, there is no reason to commission a $60,000 set of drawings before it. Each study that passes raises the probability that the project is sound, and each one you skip leaves a probability you are carrying blind. Write the sequence down at the start, with an estimated cost and an estimated value for each step, and revise it as results arrive.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is skipping the study because the deal feels urgent, the seller is pressing and the study takes three weeks. Urgency is a cost the seller would like you to pay. The control is to make the study a written criterion of the land gate, to write down the probability and the possible loss, and to compute the ceiling. If the seller will not wait for a study worth more than it costs, that refusal is itself information.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner sees a study as an expense against profit. The professional sees it as insurance priced against an expected loss, and judges it by the decision it can change. A study that cannot change your decision, whatever it finds, is not worth buying at any price.

Callback

In lesson 2, Ford showed Berlin, where the owner kept accepting changes and holding a date with no gate to stop it. Expected value is the arithmetic of a gate. Had someone priced the expected cost of each change and each month against the value of stopping to integrate the design properly, the gate would have looked cheap.

Recap

Expected value weighs each outcome by its probability. Compare the decision with and without the gate; the difference is the gate's value. The cost at which a perfect study stops paying is the expected value of perfect information. Check survivability as well as averages, and question where every probability came from.

Next: Remi, The Room — the gate meeting, and every seat at the table.
checklist: Write down the probability of each major hidden problem before buying land, and say where the figure came from.
Estimate the loss if that problem is discovered after purchase.
Compute expected value with and without each proposed study.
Compute the most the study can be worth, and treat it as a ceiling.
Decline any study that could not change your decision.
Check that the worst plausible outcome is survivable, separately from the average.
Record the estimates so you can compare them with what actually happened.
head: Field checklist
speak: A gate costs money, so I price it. Expected value is each outcome times its probability, added up. On a hypothetical site with two million of profit, a twenty-five percent chance of a hidden problem and a one and a half million loss if I miss it, buying blind is worth 1.125 million on average. Spending 120,000 on studies that would find the problem raises that to 1.38 million, so the gate is worth about 255,000. The most I should pay for a perfect study is the expected loss it avoids: twenty-five percent of 1.5 million, or 375,000. Real studies are imperfect, so that is a ceiling. Two more checks. Can I survive the bad case, not just win on average? And where did my probability come from? A study that cannot change my decision is not worth buying at any price.
terms: Expected value — the average outcome of a decision, found by multiplying each possible outcome by its probability and adding the results.
Expected value of perfect information — the most it is worth paying to remove an uncertainty completely before deciding.
Survivability — whether you can absorb the worst plausible outcome of a decision, judged separately from its average.

hostile.q: You want three weeks and a hundred and twenty thousand dollars for studies. The seller has another buyer. Why should we risk losing the site?
hostile.a: Because on my numbers the studies buy about $375,000 of avoided expected loss for $120,000, and the worst case without them is a loss we would not want to carry. If the site is lost to someone willing to buy blind, that is a cost I accept.

title: The gate meeting: every seat at the table
summary: A gate meeting brings every seat at the table into one room, and each seat is paid for something different. Your job is to hold the meeting to the written criteria: ask for evidence, hear the question behind each question, stay silent after asking for a number, and refuse to let enthusiasm stand in for proof.
body:
The gate meeting is where momentum and evidence meet. Every seat at the table is paid for something different, so every voice in the room pulls in a slightly different direction. Your job is to hold the meeting to the criteria you wrote before the spend.

Recall

Q. What was Rule 1?

A. No date, announcement or sunk cost moves me past a gate. Only the gate's written criteria do.

Q. In lesson 4, what is an authority having jurisdiction?

A. The official or office with legal power to approve, inspect or enforce a particular requirement.

Q. In lesson 5, what is the most you should pay for a perfect study?

A. The expected loss it avoids, called the expected value of perfect information.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, written criteria are useless if they collapse in the room. People are persuasive, deadlines are real, and you will want the project to proceed. This lesson is a scene, the lines to say and not say, and how to hold your own state while the room leans on you.

The scene

This is a composite example. It is Thursday. Your option on a hypothetical site for 40 apartments expires on Monday, when you must either pay the full price or walk away. Your gate criteria, signed three months ago, say you proceed only if: the land-use approval for 40 units is granted; a cost estimate from a qualified cost consultant supports a profit on cost at or above the minimum you set; the soil report shows no unusual foundation cost; and a lender has issued written indicative terms.

Around the table: your architect, who has finished schematic drawings; the broker who brought you the site; your cost consultant; a representative of a lender; and your lawyer. Here is what each seat wants, not from malice but from how each is paid.

SeatHow they are paidWhat they want from this meeting
ArchitectFees by stageTo start the next design stage
BrokerCommission at closingClosing
Cost consultantFee for the estimateTo be accurate and not blamed later
LenderInterest and fees if it lendsA safe loan, or no loan
LawyerHourly or fixed feeA clean transaction you will not regret

That table is the first tool. You fill it in before every gate meeting, so that you hear each voice with its incentive attached.

Lines to say

  • "Let us go through the criteria one at a time. For each one, show me the evidence."
  • "What would have to be true for this criterion to fail?"
  • "Is that in writing?"
  • "If we do not close on Monday, what exactly do we lose?"
  • To the cost consultant: "What is the range on this estimate, and what is outside it?"

Worked example one. The cost estimate arrives and shows profit on cost one percentage point below your minimum. The architect says some savings can be found in design development. The correct line is: "Then the criterion is not met today. Show me the specific savings, priced by the cost consultant, and we will reconvene." The criterion is not "profit can probably be found"; it is the number you wrote.

Say that out loud now.

Lines never to say

  • "We have come too far to stop." That is the sunk cost talking. What you have spent does not change what the next dollar buys.
  • "The lender is basically on board." Either there are written terms or there are not.
  • "We will figure out the foundations later." Later is after you own the land.
  • "I already told people this is happening." Rule 1 exists for exactly this sentence.

The question behind the question

Worked example two. The broker asks, "Can we firm up by Friday so the seller does not get nervous?" The surface question is about the seller. The question behind it is about the commission, which is paid only if you close. That does not make the broker dishonest; it makes the broker paid on closing. Your answer: "Our option runs to Monday. We will decide on Monday against the criteria, as agreed." The lender's representative asks, "What is your equity, and when does it go in?" The question behind that is: will you still be standing if costs rise? Answer with your liquidity plan, not with optimism.

When to stay silent

After you ask for a number, stop talking. People fill silence with the truth more often than with spin, and an uncomfortable pause is often when the cost consultant adds, "Of course, that excludes the dewatering." The same applies when someone gives you an answer that does not answer the question. Say nothing, look at them, and wait. Silence is a question nobody can deflect.

Silence also applies to you. When the room offers a reason to proceed that is not one of the criteria, such as "the market is hot" or "the seller likes you", do not argue with it. Arguing gives it standing. Simply return to the list: "Noted. Next criterion." The criteria are the agenda, and everything else is conversation.

How to hold your state

You will feel pressure in your body: a faster pulse, a tight chest, an urge to agree so the discomfort ends. That is normal, and you have handled worse on a night shift. Slow down your speech, keep your hands still, and read the criteria aloud from the paper rather than from memory. Reading the written document aloud does two things: it reminds the room that the bar was set in advance, and it gives you a few seconds to think. If you are not ready to decide, say, "I will give you my decision by noon tomorrow," and leave the room. Then keep that promise exactly; a deadline you set and meet is one of the cheapest ways to build trust with everyone at the table.

Ethics and anti-corruption

Gate meetings sometimes include, or are followed by, a conversation with someone close to a public approval. A typical version is a suggestion that a permit could move faster if a particular consultant were hired, or that a "facilitation" payment is how things work locally. Treat any such suggestion as a red line, not a negotiation. Anti-bribery laws in many countries can apply to conduct abroad as well as at home, and a project built on a corrupt approval carries that risk for its whole life. Verify the laws that apply to you against the primary source, and take legal advice the same day.

The practical habit is simple. Never discuss payments to officials, never use an agent whose fee is unexplained, and write a short note of any such approach, with the date, and send it to your lawyer. Your reputation is an asset on your balance sheet, even though no accountant will ever record it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that a strong personality in the room replaces the criteria with a story. The control is to run the meeting from the written criteria, item by item, with evidence attached, and to record the outcome of each item in a short gate note signed by you.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats the gate meeting as a progress update, and the meeting ends with everyone pleased and nothing decided. A gate meeting has one output: go, no-go, or not yet, with the reason in writing.

Callback

In lesson 2, Berlin's owner held a public date long past the point the evidence supported. That happened in meetings like this one, where the most confident voice won. Your criteria are how the quietest true fact in the room beats the loudest hopeful one.

Recap

Map every seat's incentive before the meeting. Run it from the written criteria, one item at a time, asking for evidence and staying silent after the question. Never let sunk cost, an announcement or a vague lender stand in for proof. Leave with go, no-go or not yet, in writing.

Next: Kema, Quiz and Recap — the developer's job, week 1.
checklist: Fill in the incentive table for every seat before each gate meeting.
Bring the signed gate criteria and read them aloud, one item at a time.
Ask for the evidence behind each criterion, in writing.
Stay silent after asking for a number.
Answer the question behind the question, not just the surface question.
Leave with a written outcome: go, no-go or not yet, with reasons.
Record any approach involving payments to officials and send it to your lawyer the same day.
head: Field checklist
speak: In a gate meeting, every seat is paid for something different. The architect wants the next stage, the broker wants closing, the lender wants a safe loan or no loan. I fill in that incentive table before the meeting so I hear each voice with its pay attached. Then I run the meeting from the written criteria, one item at a time, and ask for the evidence. If the cost estimate is one point below my minimum, the criterion is not met today, no matter how confident the room feels. I never say we have come too far to stop. After I ask for a number, I stay silent and let the answer arrive. I hold my state by slowing down and reading the criteria aloud. The meeting ends with one output: go, no-go or not yet, written down. And any hint of a payment to speed an approval is a red line.
terms: Gate meeting — a decision meeting held at a go/no-go gate, run from the written criteria with evidence for each one.
Incentive table — a short list of each party at the table, how they are paid, and what they want from the decision.
Gate note — a short signed record of each criterion, the evidence for it, and the go, no-go or not-yet decision.

hostile.q: From the broker: if you do not firm up by Friday, the seller may go with the other buyer. Are you really prepared to lose this site over one point of margin?
hostile.a: Yes. The criterion was set before we started, and today it is not met. If the architect's savings are real, the cost consultant can price them by Monday and I will decide then. If the seller prefers another buyer, I accept that.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 1 quiz and recap: the developer's job
summary: Six questions test the week: profit as a residual, the four levers, the lifecycle, gates, the public approvals, the value of information and the gate meeting. A Red Pen drill and a two-minute boardroom drill make you use it.
body:
This week you learned what a developer is actually paid to do: carry the residual, steer three of the four levers, buy information while it is cheap, and pass each gate only on its written criteria. Today you prove it to yourself.

Recall

Q. In lesson 3, what happened to return on equity when the hypothetical project overran by 10 percent?

A. It fell from about 41 percent to about 10 percent, and the overrun arrived as a $1.4 million cash call.

Q. In lesson 1, which of the four levers does the developer not control at all?

A. The market's multiple; he only controls his exposure to it.

Q. In lesson 5, what two checks does a professional make before accepting a positive expected value?

A. That the expected value is positive, and that the worst plausible outcome is survivable.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, recognition is not recall. You recognised every idea this week as you read it. The test is whether you can produce it unprompted, in your own words, with the numbers right. Answer each question aloud before you read the answer. Speaking forces you to put the idea in order, and an idea you cannot say in order is one you will not be able to use in a room with a lender across the table. Keep a pen nearby and mark any question where you hesitated; those are the ones to revisit before next week, because week 2 builds directly on the gate and the expected-value ideas.

The six questions

Question 1. Why does a 10 percent cost overrun cut a developer's profit by far more than 10 percent?

Answer: Because profit is a residual, the small difference between value and cost. On the hypothetical $14 million building worth $16 million, a 10 percent overrun is $1.4 million, which cuts the $2 million profit by 70 percent.

Question 2. Name the four levers and say which ones you steer.

Answer: Income, cost, time and the market's multiple. You steer income, cost and time; you only manage your exposure to the multiple, through timing, leverage and the ability to wait.

Question 3. Why should gate criteria be written before the spend?

Answer: Because after the money is spent, your judgment is contaminated by sunk cost, by commitments to others and by wanting your work to matter. Writing the bar first protects the future decision.

Question 4. What was the root cause at Berlin Brandenburg Airport?

Answer: An owner acting as integrator of a complex building without the capability to do it, with no gate on changes. The failed fire and smoke system and the cancelled 2012 opening were symptoms; the defended public date made them worse.

Question 5. Name the four public gates and one duty the code may place on the owner.

Answer: Land use, building permit, inspections and occupancy. The IBC's special inspection provisions generally require the owner or the owner's agent to engage special inspectors for certain critical work; verify that against the current adopted edition.

Question 6. A study costs $50,000. There is a 20 percent chance of a problem that would cost $1 million if missed. Assuming the study reliably finds it, is it worth buying?

Answer: The expected loss it avoids is 0.2 times $1 million, which is $200,000. That is the ceiling. At $50,000, the study is worth buying, provided its result could change your decision.

Say that out loud now.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical gate memo and find the defects before you read the answers.

Gate 2 memo, hypothetical 40-unit project. Recommendation: proceed to land closing Monday. Profit is $2.6 million, which is strong. The architect confirms zoning will allow 40 units once we apply. Soil report to follow after closing. The lender is basically on board. We have already spent $180,000 and announced the project to the community, so stopping now would waste that investment. Construction start is scheduled for month 4, when the building permit will be issued.

The defects:

  1. "Profit is $2.6 million" gives no profit on cost and no sensitivity. Strong compared to what?
  2. "Zoning will allow 40 units once we apply" is a hope, not an approval, and it comes from the architect rather than the authority having jurisdiction. The approval should be granted before closing.
  3. "Soil report to follow after closing" puts the information after the commitment, the opposite of what lesson 5 taught.
  4. "The lender is basically on board" is not written terms.
  5. "We have already spent $180,000 and announced the project" is sunk cost and an announcement, which Rule 1 says cannot move you past a gate.
  6. "When the building permit will be issued" treats a public gate as a date rather than a risk.
  7. Nothing in the memo refers back to the written criteria at all.

Boardroom drill

Set a timer for two minutes and explain this week to an imaginary board of investors. Then compare with this model answer.

"A developer is paid last, so profit is a residual, and it swings hard. On a hypothetical fourteen million dollar building worth sixteen, a five percent miss on rent cuts profit by forty percent, and a ten percent overrun cuts it by seventy. Four levers move it: income, cost, time and the market's multiple. I steer the first three and manage my exposure to the fourth. Risk is highest when spending is lowest, so I buy information early, priced by expected value, before the land closes. The government holds four gates, land use, permit, inspections and occupancy, so my money sits behind them. And every one of my own gates has written criteria set before the spend. At Berlin Brandenburg Airport, an owner without the capability to integrate the job approved changes with no gate and defended a date it had not earned. It opened eight years late. My rule is that only written criteria open a gate."

How to score yourself

Give yourself one point for each question you answered aloud, correctly, before reading the answer, and one point for each Red Pen defect you found unaided. There are seven defects, so the total is out of thirteen. Below nine, reread lessons 1 and 5 tomorrow; those two carry the arithmetic the others depend on. Then repeat the boardroom drill and record it on your phone. Listen back once, and note only two things: did you lead with the bottom line, and did you get the numbers right? Do not judge your voice yet; week 4 deals with that. The aim today is accuracy and order.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is believing that knowing the rule means you will follow it under pressure. The control is rehearsal: read your criteria aloud before every gate meeting, as practice for the moment someone says the seller has another buyer.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner also treats a quiz as a test of memory. It is a test of use. If you can answer Question 6 only with the exact numbers from lesson 5, change the numbers and try again: a 10 percent chance, a $3 million loss, a $250,000 study. If the method still works for you, you own it.

The beginner reads the answers before attempting the questions. Cover the answers, speak first, then check. The discomfort of getting one wrong is what makes it stick.

Callback

In lesson 1, Remi compared gates to operating limits in grid operations: set in advance so nobody invents them under pressure. Every item in this week connects to that idea. The levers tell you what the limits protect, the public gates are limits someone else sets, expected value tells you what a limit is worth, and the gate meeting is where you hold the line.

Recap

The developer is paid last; profit is a residual moved by income, cost, time and the multiple. Measure it against cost and against equity. Buy information before land closes. Put your money behind the public gates. Price studies with expected value. Run gate meetings from written criteria. Rule 1 holds it together.

Next: Kema, First Principles — the outside view: forecasting from reference classes.
checklist: Why does a 10 percent overrun cut profit by far more than 10 percent?
What are the four levers, and which do you steer?
Why must gate criteria be written before the spend?
What was the root cause at Berlin Brandenburg Airport?
What are the four public gates, and one duty the code may place on the owner?
What is the most you should pay for a study, and when is it worth nothing?
head: The six questions
speak: This week in one minute. A developer is paid last, so profit is a residual, the small gap between value and cost, and it swings hard: on a hypothetical fourteen million dollar building worth sixteen, a ten percent overrun cuts profit by seventy percent. Four levers move it: income, cost, time and the market's multiple. I steer three; I manage my exposure to the fourth. Risk is highest when spending is lowest, so I buy information before the land closes, and I price each study by the expected loss it avoids. The government holds four gates: land use, permit, inspections and occupancy, so my money sits behind them. My own gates have written criteria set before the spend, and I run gate meetings from those criteria, item by item. Berlin Brandenburg Airport shows what happens without that. Rule 1: no date, announcement or sunk cost moves me past a gate.
terms: Residual — what is left after every fixed claim has been paid.
Go/no-go gate — a decision point opened only by criteria written before the spend.
Expected value of perfect information — the most it is worth paying to remove an uncertainty before deciding.

hostile.q: From an investor: you talk a lot about gates. Isn't all this process just a way to delay and charge more fees?
hostile.a: No. Most of the gates cost little and sit before the large commitments, where information is cheap. Each one is priced: if a study cannot change a decision, I do not buy it. The gates exist so that your money is committed on evidence rather than on momentum.
